title: Bike Check Card
user: A self-maintaining cyclist who needs to capture a fault's exact symptoms, component state, photos, and ride context before deciding whether to pause riding or ask a mechanic/community for help.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A rider asks for an alarm when wheel-sensor speed materially disagrees with GPS after intermittent sensor failure; the present app silently reports only the bad reading.
A rider documents pressure, mileage, visible fibres, and riding plans while asking whether a damaged tyre can still be used—exactly the facts that are otherwise scattered across a post.

recurrence: Two independent 2025 threads expose the same high-stakes capture problem: a defect or conflicting reading must be described accurately before someone can help. Severity is high because an incomplete record can lead to a wasted shop visit or an unsafe ride.
current_workaround: Take ad-hoc phone photos, write a long forum post, and try to remember pressure, mileage, and sensor readings.
incumbents_and_gap: Strava and Garmin record rides; OpenTracks records tracks; bike-maintenance apps schedule services. None gives a fast, shareable, component-aware fault card with evidence and no safety verdict.
smallest_useful_product: Offline form for bike, component, mileage, pressure, symptom timeline, sensor-vs-GPS reading, and annotated photos; exports a single private link/PDF. Non-goals: diagnosing safety, recommending replacement, telemetry ingestion, or social feeds.
success_measure: In a 20-cyclist test, at least 12 create and share a complete check card in under four minutes, with at least 80% containing bike, component, symptom, and one measurement.
monetization: one-time — a privacy-first utility is valuable at the moment of a real problem and should not hold safety records hostage to a subscription.
constraints: Make the no-safety-advice boundary explicit; keep photos local until the user exports; avoid claiming compatibility with a component manufacturer's warranty process.
why_distinct: This is an evidence-capture and handoff tool, not another ride tracker or maintenance reminder.

title: Route Fidelity Check
user: A cyclist or club ride leader who has a deliberate GPX route and needs to know whether a navigation app/device silently rerouted it before riders follow it.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A walking-club route creator says automatic completion reconnects waypoints on a nonsensical path and requests that only segments between deliberate waypoints be optimized.
A RideWithGPS route containing a rail trail becomes nearby roads after the Garmin handoff despite the trail being visible in Garmin's map.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–2026 route-authoring reports describe route mutation at the handoff layer. Severity is high for group rides because the leader may discover a bad route only while navigating.
current_workaround: Manually inspect the route in each app/device, add many shaping points, or discover the deviation after export.
incumbents_and_gap: RideWithGPS, Garmin Connect, Komoot, and Organic Maps plan routes, but each owns its routing engine. There is no neutral, tiny preflight that compares an intended GPX line with an exported/re-rendered line.
smallest_useful_product: Browser tool that accepts two GPX files, aligns them, highlights divergences over a user-set distance, and emits a printable cue/checklist. Non-goals: route planning, turn-by-turn navigation, accounts, or map-data editing.
success_measure: On a 30-pair corpus of planned and exported GPX files, the tool flags 90% of known material detours and produces a reviewable result in under 15 seconds.
monetization: free — it is a focused trust-building utility that can seed later paid club export packs if demand appears.
constraints: Process GPX locally; use permissively licensed base-map tiles only if a map preview is included; clearly distinguish geometric difference from a claim that a route is safe or legal.
why_distinct: It audits a route handoff instead of competing to be the next route planner.

title: Game Night Score Ledger
user: A board-game host running games with score tracks that wrap, teams, or many rounds who needs an auditable scoreboard that does not interrupt play.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A current board-game tracker explicitly requests a game-night page for creating and managing RSVPs, showing that play-session support is separate from a collection catalog.
A Stone Age player cannot track laps once the physical 0–99 score track wraps and resorts to borrowing Carcassonne lap counters.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 requests show session administration and score-overflow failures during play. Severity is medium-high: the physical game state becomes disputed or cumbersome at the table.
current_workaround: Paper, borrowed counters, a generic calculator, or a large all-purpose collection app.
incumbents_and_gap: BoardGameGeek logs plays, and BG Stats has broad tracking. Neither is optimized for a one-screen, no-account, table-facing ledger with laps, teams, and an exportable event receipt.
smallest_useful_product: A share-by-QR PWA: host enters players, scoring increments, optional lap threshold, and team totals; guests can view but not edit; export CSV/image. Non-goals: game rules engines, BGG catalog sync, chat, ratings, or ads.
success_measure: At least 15 of 20 test sessions finish with a saved score record and no manual recalculation, while first setup takes under 60 seconds.
monetization: one-time — hosts can reasonably pay for a polished offline table tool, without forcing players into accounts.
constraints: Support local-first shared state and conflict-safe host controls; do not reproduce copyrighted game rules or artwork.
why_distinct: A session instrument for awkward physical scoreboards, not a collection database or generic score-counter clone.

title: Shelf Rotation Picklist
user: A board gamer with a growing shelf who wants a fair, practical next-play shortlist based on neglect, player count, setup burden, and what is actually available tonight.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The feature request is concise and direct: show games not played in over x months.
An organizer with 2,000+ bulk cards calls sorting and entering them into a collection app a nightmare while trying to make a fun event from what they already own.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–2026 organizers have surplus inventory but lack a lightweight way to turn it into an actionable session choice. Severity is medium: the result is unused purchases and planning friction.
current_workaround: Scroll a collection, spin a randomizer, use a spreadsheet, or never revisit the shelf-of-shame.
incumbents_and_gap: BoardGameGeek and BG Stats retain ownership/play data; generic randomizers ignore setup, players, and event constraints. The gap is an explainable shortlist rather than another catalog.
smallest_useful_product: Local CSV/manual import of title, last-played, player range, minutes, setup friction, and tags; filters tonight's constraints and creates a 3–5 game rotation with a visible reason for each pick. Non-goals: recommendations from scraped ratings, marketplace prices, or full collection management.
success_measure: Among 25 collectors, 60% who import at least 20 games save a generated shortlist twice within 30 days.
monetization: free — the narrow transparent picker has a low support burden and can validate whether paid family/club shared shelves are wanted.
constraints: Do not scrape BoardGameGeek or use its branding/data without permission; imports must be user-provided; make the scoring rule inspectable rather than LLM-generated.
why_distinct: It converts neglected owned items into a constraint-aware play plan, rather than duplicating a game library.

title: Boardgame Session Notes
user: A game group that wants a compact record of a particular play—starting state, disputes, house rules, score laps, and outcomes—without losing it when an item leaves the collection.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A current BoardGamesCompanion task preserves import progress/retry/backoff because users otherwise have to babysit a queued BoardGameGeek collection import.
A Skat player asks how to reconstruct an initial hand after tricks are collected because the information is lost and nobody can reliably remember it.

recurrence: These two independent reports show that catalog history and in-session state are both fragile: import pipelines are unreliable, while physical information disappears after play. Severity is medium for groups that revisit games or settle disputes.
current_workaround: Trust memory, keep paper notes, or rely on a remote collection import to be available at the table.
incumbents_and_gap: BoardGameGeek/BG Stats retain broad play logs; rulebook apps explain rules. Neither offers a local, game-agnostic session notebook that starts from a pasted title and survives catalog deletion or API outages.
smallest_useful_product: Offline session template with participants, pre-play state/photo, reusable house-rule snippets, event timeline, and final score; export a single Markdown/PDF receipt. Non-goals: rules lookup, automated scoring, BGG import, or replacing a campaign manager.
success_measure: In 15 repeat groups, at least 10 reopen a prior session note during a subsequent play or rules discussion within six weeks.
monetization: one-time — durable local records are a clear paid utility without network service costs.
constraints: Do not distribute rule text, game art, or community data; keep notes local by default and make exports user-controlled.
why_distinct: It protects ephemeral session context, not another online collection or rules encyclopedia.

title: Metadata Change Receipt
user: A photographer or small archive manager who needs to batch-plan and verify date, caption, keyword, and IPTC edits without trusting a black-box library import job.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A fresh Immich instance with roughly 460,000 assets sees the metadata-extraction queue grow to about 650,000 and never drain, making the library's metadata state untrustworthy.
A Lightroom user with large sets asks for tools or plug-ins to automate titles, captions, and keywords directly into IPTC because manual work is too time-consuming.

recurrence: One 2025 professional-style batch-edit request and one large-library extraction failure show a recurring trust problem: photographers cannot easily prove what metadata should have changed. Severity rises sharply with library size.
current_workaround: Run Lightroom/ExifTool/import jobs, inspect random files, and keep a separate spreadsheet of intended changes.
incumbents_and_gap: Lightroom Classic, Immich, PhotoPrism, and ExifTool can change or extract fields. The unresolved gap is a human-readable before/after receipt and exception list independent of a catalog vendor.
smallest_useful_product: Local desktop-web workflow that accepts exported metadata CSVs, defines a field transformation, previews affected rows, and produces a signed before/after receipt plus exceptions CSV. Non-goals: writing image files, AI captioning, cloud DAM, or replacing Lightroom.
success_measure: At least 90% of a 10,000-row fixture's intended edits are represented exactly once in the receipt, and users can identify every exception without opening individual images.
monetization: one-time — auditability is a bounded, professional utility and does not require a hosted account.
constraints: Run entirely client-side; protect filenames/location data; clearly state that CSV verification does not prove pixels or embedded XMP were written.
why_distinct: It is an audit layer around existing metadata tools, not a photo organizer or thin AI tagger.

title: RAW Sidecar Sanity
user: A photographer importing RAW plus camera JPEG pairs who needs to catch impossible dimensions, aspect ratios, or timestamps before a catalog makes bad thumbnails and timelines.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Sony ARW import is reported as 5120×7168 instead of 4672×7008, while the camera JPEG sidecar is correct; the user observes visible aspect-ratio distortion.
After correcting EXIF dates with ExifTool, a camera still displays the old date/category, illustrating that a seemingly fixed metadata field can disagree across consumers.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 cases show consumer disagreement over fundamental photo facts: dimensions/aspect in one and capture dates in another. Severity is high before a bulk import because errors propagate into derived previews and folders.
current_workaround: Open files one by one in several apps, compare against JPEGs, or discover defects after catalog import.
incumbents_and_gap: ExifTool exposes fields and DAMs show their own interpretation. No lightweight preflight focuses on pairwise contradictions and clearly says which reader reported what.
smallest_useful_product: Local drag-and-drop checker for a folder manifest or selected RAW/JPEG pairs; reports dimension, aspect, timestamp, and basename conflicts with a CSV export. Non-goals: decoding every RAW, correcting metadata, importing to a DAM, or cloud upload.
success_measure: On a labelled corpus of 200 valid and intentionally mismatched pairs, detect at least 95% of injected date/aspect/basename conflicts with under 3% false positives.
monetization: one-time — preflight is occasional but has clear value when an archive is at risk.
constraints: Browser RAW parsing coverage will be incomplete; document supported metadata readers; never modify originals; avoid retaining image bytes.
why_distinct: It checks agreement among files and readers before import instead of becoming a photo catalog.

title: Photo Stack Proof
user: An iPhone/RAW photographer with years of exports who needs to verify that same-name images, videos, and sidecars really belong together before a DAM stacks or deletes them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: PhotoPrism users request embedded content-identifier verification because name-only grouping can merge unrelated rollover files into one card with mismatched thumbnails, labels, and Live Photo previews.
A photographer cannot choose between two similarly named DateTimeOriginal tags and asks which reliably records when a JPEG was captured.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 reports show that filename and a single timestamp are weak identity signals. Severity is high because false stacks can make distinct originals appear as one asset.
current_workaround: Trust the DAM's grouping, rename files manually, or inspect EXIF fields with specialist tools.
incumbents_and_gap: PhotoPrism, Lightroom, Immich, and Apple Photos stack media, but their grouping logic is not a portable proof report users can run before import or deletion.
smallest_useful_product: Local analyser that groups candidate pairs by basename, reads available capture/content IDs and timestamps, and labels each as verified, ambiguous, or conflict; exports a review CSV. Non-goals: auto-merge/delete, a DAM, face recognition, or cloud backups.
success_measure: On 100 labelled candidate groups, correctly separate at least 90% of deliberately colliding basenames and never mark a conflict group safe without a matching strong identifier.
monetization: one-time — users pay for a careful preflight before a migration, not ongoing hosting.
constraints: Never delete or rename files; content-ID support varies by format; describe heuristic confidence honestly; keep potentially sensitive metadata on-device.
why_distinct: It is a conservative identity-verification tool, not another automatic photo-stacking feature.

title: Practice Next Card
user: A self-directed musician who needs to leave a precise, encouraging next action at a troublesome measure instead of accumulating paper notes or stalling between lessons.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A musician asks for a score comment pop-up for notes such as “fix bar 37”; today they write reminders on scraps of paper.
After losing affordable instruction, a musician says unguided practice of scales/exercises drains enjoyment and they have hit a skill wall.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 musicians describe missing continuity between sessions: one loses measure-specific reminders, another loses direction without a teacher. Severity is high enough to stop regular practice.
current_workaround: Paper scraps, generic to-do lists, memory, or a broad habit tracker detached from the actual piece.
incumbents_and_gap: MuseScore stores notation and many practice apps count minutes. The gap is a tiny local queue of measure-specific next actions, evidence of attempts, and an end-of-session handoff—not a lesson platform.
smallest_useful_product: Offline cards with piece name, measure/range, one next action, timer, perceived outcome, and optional photo/link to the user's own score; show only today's 3 cards. Non-goals: score hosting, AI feedback, metronome, social coaching, or copyrighted sheet-music distribution.
success_measure: In a four-week pilot, at least 60% of activated users complete two or more cards per week and reopen a prior card at least once.
monetization: one-time — the product holds personal practice notes and should remain usable offline without a subscription.
constraints: Do not ingest or redistribute copyrighted scores; store only user-entered measure references; avoid health/skill-improvement claims.
why_distinct: It captures the next concrete action at the music, rather than merely tracking streaks or generating advice.

title: Rehearsal Section Cues
user: A small ensemble leader or multi-instrument player who needs a clear, printable cue sheet for where a rehearsal section begins, who plays on each pass, and what is difficult there.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A notation user asks for previous/next rehearsal-mark hints and jumping because, after moving to a random point in a piece, they are often disoriented about exactly where they are.
A player considering a fast solo asks how to decide independently whether a passage is realistically learnable before committing serious practice.

recurrence: One 2025 readiness question and one active 2026 navigation request expose the same rehearsal-planning gap: the score alone does not state the practical work at each section. Severity is medium-high for limited rehearsal time.
current_workaround: Markup on photocopies, separate emails, or trying to encode rehearsal intent into notation software.
incumbents_and_gap: MuseScore, forScore, and Setlist apps manage scores/setlists. They do not produce a fast, score-agnostic section cue card that an ensemble can agree on without editing the source notation.
smallest_useful_product: A printable/mobile cue-sheet builder: section label, repeat number, active players, one technical risk, tempo target, and completion status. Non-goals: score rendering, playback, automated difficulty scoring, cloud rehearsal rooms, or copyrighted chart storage.
success_measure: In 10 ensemble rehearsals, leaders create a usable sheet in under eight minutes and participants report fewer than one clarification per repeated section on average.
monetization: one-time — an ensemble-friendly print/export utility has clear event value with no ongoing infrastructure need.
constraints: Use only user-entered section labels and measure references; do not host sheet music; support accessible high-contrast printable output.
why_distinct: It lives beside notation as a rehearsal-operating sheet, not as a competing notation editor.

title: Catch Photo Log
user: An angler who takes a catch photo and needs a fast, private record of where/when it happened plus the tackle and setup facts useful on the next trip.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A fishing-journal user explicitly requests that a selected catch photo populate time, date, and location from its metadata, falling back to manual entry only when absent.
An angler trying a 100-metre trotline records line, snood, weight, target fish, lake, and fairway context while asking how to choose an anchor—trip setup is materially more than a catch count.

recurrence: Two independent 2025–2026 fishing threads require structured field capture: photo facts for one and detailed rig/site context for the other. Severity is medium because remembered details are what make a trip learnable.
current_workaround: Camera roll plus notes, spreadsheet, a social catch app, or re-entering GPS/date manually.
incumbents_and_gap: Fishbrain and Anglr emphasize community, maps, and catch feeds; generic logbooks record catches. The gap is a local photo-first session card that preserves detailed setup without exposing a fishing spot.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA that reads optional photo EXIF, then prompts for species, rig, bait/lure, water conditions, line/anchor setup, and private location precision; exports CSV/PDF. Non-goals: fish identification, bite prediction, social feed, public maps, or regulatory advice.
success_measure: At least 70% of 30 trial session records retain a photo-derived time/date plus three manually chosen setup fields, with median entry time under 90 seconds.
monetization: one-time — private, offline field records are credible as a small paid companion and avoid funding through location-data exploitation.
constraints: Location must be private and removable/rounded; never advise on catch limits or anchoring safety; EXIF access requires explicit browser permission and local processing.
why_distinct: It is a private learning log for rig/context, not another public catch map or AI fish-ID wrapper.

title: Bird Sighting Proof Card
user: A birder with an uncertain observation who needs to package photo, sound, time, location precision, field marks, and identification uncertainty for later review without oversharing sensitive locations.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A bird-tracking team wants metadata from separate GPS-tracker technology sheets combined because managing fragmented observation metadata is difficult.
A birder with distant photos and inconclusive Merlin sound/photo suggestions cannot distinguish fulmars from kittiwakes and supplies date, place, and observation context.

recurrence: Two 2026 bird-data cases show that observation evidence is fragmented across photos, tools, tracker metadata, and memory. Severity is medium-high: uncertainty remains unresolved and sensitive site data may be shared too broadly.
current_workaround: Post a prose description with attachments, keep separate spreadsheets, or rely on an identification app's single suggestion.
incumbents_and_gap: Merlin and eBird identify/record birds; research platforms manage tracking data. The gap is a tool-neutral evidence packet that records uncertainty and deliberately controls location precision before sharing.
smallest_useful_product: Offline proof-card builder with photo/audio attachments, extracted timestamp, rounded location options, field-mark checklist, candidate/confidence notes, and shareable PDF/JSON. Non-goals: automated species identification, public sighting map, eBird submission, or research GPS management.
success_measure: In a 20-card pilot, 80% of shared cards include date, precision-controlled place, one evidence attachment, and an explicit confidence level; no exported card includes exact coordinates unless the user opts in.
monetization: free — a privacy-respecting evidence format can earn trust first and has negligible recurring cost.
constraints: Sensitive-species and nesting locations require safe defaults; do not imply an identification is authoritative; user media and coordinates remain local until export.
why_distinct: It improves the quality and safety of uncertain observations without pretending to replace bird-identification or citizen-science networks.
